### Physiology

Membrane voltages in each simulated compartment were calculated using the standard Hodgkin-Huxley parallel conductance equations, and current flow between compartments follows from cable theory as accounted for in NEURON.

Extending the prior work of Bush and Sejnowski (1993), active ionic currents were included in both the somatic and dendritic compartment of the cells of the pyramidal neurons, and in the single compartment of the inhibitory neurons. For the pyramidal neurons, the membrane resistance was increased and membrane capacitance was decreased from the Bush and Sejnowski’s values by the same 1.3 scaling factor as the compartment sizes described above (Rm23,474 cm2 for L5 and L2/3; Cm 0.85 and Cm0.6195 F/cm2 for L5 and L2/3, respectively) to maintain the input resistances in the cells of 45 M for the L5 and 110 M for L2/3 (Douglas et al., 1991). The axial resistance for each cell was Ra200 cm (Segev et al., 1992). The parameters regulating the active currents were tuned to replicate known in vitro firing patterns in response to somatic current injection.

### Local network connections

HNN’s default template neocortical model includes neurons arranged in three dimensions. The XY plane is used to array cells on a regular grid while the Z-axis specifies cortical layer. HNN’s default model contains a regular 10 × 10 grid (arbitrary units) of pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 and layer five for a total of 200 pyramidal neurons, with interneurons interleaved regularly in a 3–1 ratio (see Figure 3D). The local synaptic architecture in Figure 3A was based on an abundance of animal studies and, in particular, studies of the mouse/rat somatosensory cortex (Bernardo et al., 1990a; Bernardo et al., 1990b; for review, see Thomson et al., 2002; Thomson and Bannister, 2003, and Bannister, 2005). Inhibitory synaptic connections onto PNs were located on the soma (Freund et al., 1986; Kisvárday et al., 1985; Somogyi et al., 1983), and excitatory synapses contacted the basal and apical oblique dendrites (Deuchars et al., 1994; Feldmeyer et al., 2002; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson and Bannister, 1998).

Synaptic dynamics were modeled with bi-exponential functions. The rise and decay time constants and reversal potentials were based on experiments and the original neocortical model in Jones et al. (2009), and are generally as follows: AMPA (0.5 ms, 1.0 ms, 0 mV); NMDA (1.0 ms, 20.0 ms, 0 mV); GABAA (0.5 ms, 5.0 ms, −80 mV), GABAB (1.0 ms, 20.0 ms, −80 mV). Within a cortical layer there is recurrent connectivity between neurons of a given type (PN to PN, interneuron to interneuron), PN to interneuron connectivity, and synaptic inhibition from interneurons onto PNs. The following synaptic connections are present across cortical layers: layer 2/3 PNs to layer 5 PNs, layer 2/3 interneurons to layer 5 PNs, layer 2/3 PNs to layer five interneurons.

The conductance of the synaptic connections within the local network grid were defined with a symmetric 2D Gaussian spatial profile, with a delay incorporate into the synaptic connection between two cells defined by and inverse Gaussian (Jones, 1986; Kaas and Garraghty, 1991). There is all-to-all connectivity between any two populations of synaptically-coupled neurons. Synaptic weights between the neurons are scaled inversely by the distance in the XY plane (arbitrary units) between the neurons ($d$) using exponential fall-off following $e^{-d^{2}/\lambda^{2}}$, and space constant $\lambda$, which depends on pre- and post-synaptic type (Table 2 below).

### Exogenous driving inputs

At rest, the default model does not generate activity. HNN provides several ways to activate the local cortical column with layer specific excitatory synaptic input representing thalamo-cortical, and/or cortical-cortical and noisy/tonic drive. The user defines the choice of driving input to the network, based on their simulation experiment, as described in Results.

Exogenous driving networks are not explicitly modeled, rather the user defines trains or bursts of action potentials representing these inputs that excite the local network via AMPA or NMDA synaptic connections to distinct layers and cellular compartments. These inputs are referred to as proximal and distal drive based on the PN dendritic contact location. Proximal inputs contact basal and oblique dendrites of PN and somas of the inhibitory neurons in L2/3 and L5, and distal inputs contact distal dendrites of the PN in L2/3 and L5 and somas of the inhibitory neurons in L2/3 only, as shown in Figure 3.

The trains of action potentials, or tonic/noisy input, that the user defines are created in specific dialog boxes in the GUI and represent either Evoked, Rhythmic, Tonic, or Poisson Inputs, as motivated by our prior studies and tutorials described in Results.

Tonic inputs are modeled as somatic current clamps with a fixed current amplitude (nA). Noisy Inputs are trains of action potentials that follow a Poisson Process and create excitatory AMPA or NMDA synaptic inputs to the somata of all neurons of a given type. ### Calculation of primary electrical current (Net Current Dipole)

Axial current flow between any two neighboring model compartments i,j is defined as iaxial = (vi - vj)/raxial, where vi, vj, and raxial are the voltages in compartment i, j, and the resistance between the compartments, respectively. In order to convert this axial current into a dipole signal, we apply a length scaling where the axial current is scaled by the inter-compartment distance along the vertical axis. The length scaling means that for the longer apical dendrites of layer five pyramidal neurons, the contribution will be larger than from the shorter layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron apical dendrites. Note that the orientation of the dendrites relative to the vertical axis also influences the contribution to the dipole signal. For example, the horizontally-oriented oblique dendrites which do not have any vertical length component, do not contribute to the dipole signal, whereas for basal dendrites oriented at 45 degrees from the vertical axis, the scaling is $-\sqrt{2}/2$ (note the negative sign is because these dendrites are pointing downward). The contribution from all neighboring compartments within a neuron is integrated and then added to a value across the set of all pyramidal neurons. As a result of the multiplication between axial current and length, the model dipole output signal has the same units of measure as the experimental data (Am) (Okada et al., 1997; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Jones et al., 2007; Hagen et al., 2018).

### ERP optimization tools

HNN includes a method to optimize ERP simulations. The optimization procedure was uniquely designed to minimize the RMSE between model output and ERP waveforms in a stepwise manner that decreases parameter exploration and saves compute time. This procedure takes advantage of the assumption that the exogenous proximal and distal driving inputs are essential parameters to tune to get an accurate representation of an ERP waveform. Additionally, it applies the knowledge that, with probabilistic certainty, features of the dipole waveform at a particular point in time cannot be influenced by an exogenous driving input that begins after that point in time.

Since exogenous inputs are modeled as Gaussian processes, the likelihood of occurrence can be modeled by a probability distribution function (PDF) normally distributed with a given mean and standard deviation. Figure 11—figure supplement 1A shows the PDFs of the inputs for the suprathreshold example described in the results Figure 11. An input’s contribution to the ERP will begin when there is a non-zero probability of occurrence and persist for a duration commensurate with the input’s cumulative distribution function (CDF), shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1B. This clearly illustrates that from 20 to 50 ms, the input labeled ‘Proximal 1’ is the unique contributor to the waveform. After 50 ms, effects from Distal one begin, thus adding new parameters that contribute to the waveform fit and reduce the relative contribution of Proximal 1 (from full to partial). It follows that each successive driving input will have a time window where it is most likely to have a unique and dominant effect. As such, our approach to model optimization is to divide the process into smaller steps where only a single input’s parameters are estimated before proceeding to optimize the next input.

To implement this procedure, we developed a new goodness of fit measure that amplifies the importance of maximizing the fit at points of unique contribution (e.g. 20–50 ms for Proximal 1, Figure 11—figure supplement 1C) and diminished the importance of fitting to later points where other inputs contribute more to the fit. We began with standard root mean squared error (RMSE)

$$
RMSE=\sqrt{\frac{\sumt=0T(x_{1,t}−x_{2,t})^{2}}{T}}
$$

where t is the current simulation time, from 0 to simulation completion (T), and x1,t is the simulated dipole at t, and x2,t is the experimental data point. Then we adapted RMSE to include weight functions specific for input k at time t,

$$
wRMSE_{k}=\sqrt{\frac{\sumt=0Tw_{k}(t)(x_{1,t}−x_{2,t})^{2}}{\sumt=0Tw_{k}(t)}}
$$

where an assignment of wk(t)=1 for all t would be equivalent to RMSE.

For each input k, we first defined a weight distribution function, wk(t), as the Unique Contribution Index (UCI), which starts from the CDF of input k and simply subtracts the CDF of subsequent inputs, with a lower bound of 0 (Figure 11—figure supplement 1C). Equivalently,

$$
UCI_{k}(t)=CDF_{k}(t)−\sumi=k+1NCDF_{i}(t),
$$

where N is the number of exogenous driving inputs in the simulation. Figure 11—figure supplement 1C shows that Proximal 1’s influence is unique up to 50 ms, Distal one has a dominant, but not unique contribution near 70 ms, and Proximal two is dominant after ~100 ms. When the UCI is applied as a weighting function in the wRMSE equation above, we observed that some optimization steps would negatively impact the fit in regions after the peak in UCI, where the errors had been down-weighted, requiring subsequent optimization steps to attempt to ‘correct’ the fit. Our solution was to instead define the weight function using the Extended Contribution Index (ECI), which includes a term that delays the weight function’s return to 0, extending the window of data points that have an impact on wRMSE further into the simulation. This achieves a balance between optimal parameter estimates for the current step and providing a good starting point for following optimization steps. ECI is defined by

$$
ECI_{k}(t)=CDF_{k}(t)−\sumi=k+1NCDF_{i}(t)A(\frac{\mu_{i}−\mu_{k}}{T}),
$$

where μi and μk are the mean start times of the next input and the current input, respectively. Simulation length is represented by T and A is an empirically derived constant. We arrived at a value of 1.6 for A as a factor that appropriately minimized the contribution of inputs proportional to the delay between their onset and the kth input currently being optimized. The effect of the ECI’s decay term can be seen in Figure 11—figure supplement 1D where the ECI for Proximal one extends further than the corresponding UCI, and the ECI of Distal one remains significant through the end of the simulation. Since points where ECIk,t approximately equal 0 will have a negligible impact on wRMSEk, we define a threshold of 0.01 where wRMSEk is calculated for the window starting when ECIk,t rises above 0.01 and ending when ECIk,t drops below 0.01. For the first exogenous driving input, it is likely that the window will end before the completion of the simulation. In that first step, simulations can be stopped early, reducing the time required for simulating each candidate parameter set in that step.

The final step in our model optimization process is to vary all free parameters from all inputs using regular RMSE to measure goodness of fit. Like each previous step, the number of simulations run is limited. So this primary purpose of this final step is to make small corrections, not perform all-at-once optimization (which would likely require thousands of simulations). It also provides an opportunity to rebalance the contributions from multiple inputs in regions where there is a high degree of parameter inter-dependence. However, if the user is certain that they want to perform all-at-once optimization (which would likely require many more simulations), they could set the number of simulations for all steps except the last one to 0, and specify a very large number of simulations for the final step.

For each optimization step, HNN uses the COBYLA optimization algorithm (Powell, 1994), which supports bound constraints as defined by the user for each parameter. We have found COBYLA converges at a local minimum faster than the PRAXIS algorithm (Brent, 1973) as implemented in NEURON’s multiple run fitter.

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The HNN provides an intuitive way for thinking about and linking cellular- and circuit-level mechanisms in the neocortex to (source-reconstructed) neural data. Combined with the worked examples that demonstrate the application of the tool to current issues, the reviewers unanimously agreed on its relevance and potential for opening up new possibilities for the field to advance our understanding of cellular and network origins of MEG/EEG data.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN), a new software tool for interpreting the cellular and network origin of human MEG/EEG data" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Arjen Stolk as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Sarang S. Dalal (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

All reviewers and editors agreed on the methodological sophistication and relevance of your software tool. However, several concerns were raised, which are summarized below. We are aware that these may be challenging to address within the usual timeframe but we all agreed that if these issues can be addressed satisfactorily, the paper would substantially improve.

Essential revisions:

1) MEG is generally considered to arise from intracellular currents, with EEG arising from extracellular currents (e.g., section 2.1 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0896627313009203). In the case of MEG, the volume currents largely cancel out, which is thought to leave intracellular currents as the main contributor to MEG signals. But volume currents are supposed to be a dominating factor in EEG, so this theoretically leads to its bias towards extracellular currents. However, the manuscript and software appear to address only intracellular currents, while MEG and EEG are discussed as if they are equivalent. This may be a necessary compromise, or the authors may disagree with the premise of MEG from intracellular and EEG from extracellular currents. However, they should be clear on their position and how this issue is handled in HNN.

2) It is a bit unsatisfying that the "Gamma rhythms" example does not use real data, given its importance to the community. Even if the authors' own experiments have not yielded data with strong gamma, there are many examples in the literature that could perhaps be obtained, and even some appropriate datasets are publicly available. For example, FieldTrip's gamma source localization tutorial provides one:

http://www.fieldtriptoolbox.org/tutorial/beamformingextended/

3) The HNN framework seems well-suited for evoked responses that are phase-locked across trials. However, gamma oscillations are often "induced", i.e., not phase-locked across trials. Does HNN provide tools to model/simulate the origins of such phase variance? If so, this should be clarified, and if not, perhaps described as a limitation.

4) There appears to be a distinction between narrowband and broadband gamma in terms of their neural underpinnings, with broadband gamma suggested to be closely linked to spiking activity (e.g. Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009 among others). Likewise, this should be described if HNN can model this, and otherwise addressed as a limitation.

5) The "jet" colormaps for the spectrograms (Figures 6 and 7) have been heavily criticized in recent years for being extremely biased perceptually (see, e.g., https://predictablynoisy.com/makeitpop-intro). In the case of Figure 6, this results in yellow patches that "pop" somewhat misleadingly. New releases of neuroscientific software should be especially cognizant of this and ideally provide a perceptually uniform colormap as the default. See https://matplotlib.org/3.1.1/tutorials/colors/colormaps.html and https://matplotlib.org/cmocean/ for some ideas on divergent colormaps.

6) The manuscript refers to previous work by the authors for details of the biophysical model. However, it is not clear from the present manuscript how well these models compare to actual experimental data and from which species the data was obtained. For example, because the model appears to use reduced and simplified neuronal morphologies, and only a single type of inhibitory interneuron, it would be very informative to provide some assessment of whether any potential inaccuracies in the generated field potentials could exist due to reduced dendritic morphology, and whether incorporation of additional inhibitory circuitry could expand the scope of questions that could be addressed via HNN.

7) The manuscript refers several times to source localization, but the presented model appears to be of a single cortical column, and presumably, this means that it is currently not possible to study questions related to the spatial distribution of field potentials. While I have no doubt that the methods of HNN will scale well to networks of multiple cortical columns, some clarity is necessary in manuscript regarding the current capability of HNN with regards to spatially distributed networks and source localization features, and what plans are made for future releases.

8) While the manuscript addresses related work by other authors, there are now several published large-scale biophysical neural models that incorporate some form of approximated LFP computation that aids the study of neural oscillations. It would be very informative to include at least a brief comparison with e.g. the methods developed by Reimann et al., 2013, and in what ways HNN is an improvement.

claims.source: The primary currents set up a potential distribution (V) that extends through the brain tissue, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the skull, and the scalp, where it is measured as EEG; the passive JV is proportional to the electric field (negative gradient of V) and electrical conductivity (σ).
claims.evidence: This describes the biophysical basis of EEG generation based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: MEG is generated by both the primary current (Jp) and volume current (Jv).
claims.source: MEG, in general, is generated by both the Jp and Jv.
claims.evidence: This is based on established electromagnetic biophysics.

claims.claim: The direction of the primary current is determined by the cellular level geometry of the active cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, the direction of the primary current is determined by the cellular level geometry of the active cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claims.claim: A spherically symmetric conductor model can often be used for MEG forward modeling.
claims.source: Specifically, a first order approximation, the spherically symmetric conductor model (Sarvas, 1987), can often be used (Tarkiainen et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on MEG forward modeling.

claims.claim: In a spherically symmetric conductor model, all components of the magnetic field can be computed from an analytical formula which is independent of the value of the electrical conductivity as a function of the distance from the center of the sphere.
claims.source: In this case, all components of the magnetic field can be computed from an analytical formula which is independent of the value of the electrical conductivity as a function of the distance from the center of the sphere (Sarvas, 1987).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The inverse problem of estimating primary current activity from MEG and EEG sensor data is fundamentally ill-posed.
claims.source: However, this inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed, and constraints are needed to render the problem unique.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established principle in EEG/MEG source estimation.

claims.claim: The appropriate elementary primary current source in all source estimation methods is estimated as a current dipole, with units current x distance, that is Am (Ampere x meter).
claims.source: Importantly, due to physiological considerations, the appropriate elementary primary current source in all of these methods is estimated as a current dipole, with units current x distance, that is Am (Ampere x meter).
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claims.claim: The primary current is oriented normal to the cortical mantle and its direction corresponds to the intracellular current flow.
claims.source: Thanks to the consistent orientation of the apical dendrites of the pyramidal cells in the cortex this primary current is oriented normal to the cortical mantle and its direction corresponds to the intracellular current flow (Okada et al., 1997; Ikeda et al., 2005; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on the biophysical basis of EEG/MEG.

claims.claim: HNN simulates the primary current from a canonical model of a layered neocortical column via the net intracellular electrical current flow in the pyramidal neuron dendrites in a direction parallel to the apical dendrites.
claims.source: Specifically, HNN simulates the primary current from a canonical model of a layered neocortical column via the net intracellular electrical current flow in the pyramidal neuron dendrites in a direction parallel to the apical dendrites (see red arrow in Figures 1 and 2, and further discussion in Materials and methods) (Hämäläinen et al., 1993; Ikeda et al., 2005; Jones, 2015; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Okada et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This describes how HNN simulates primary currents and is supported by citations and figures.

claims.claim: The units of measure produced by the HNN model are the same as those estimated from source localization methods, namely, ampere-meters (Am).
claims.source: With this construction, the units of measure produced by the model are the same as those estimated from source localization methods, namely, ampere-meters (Am), enabling one-to-one comparison of results.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the HNN model design.

claims.claim: HNN is currently constructed to dissect the cell and network contributions to signals from one source-localized region of interest.
claims.source: HNN is currently constructed to dissect the cell and network contributions to signals from one source-localized region of interest.
claims.evidence: This describes the current scope of HNN.

claims.claim: HNN's underlying neocortical network represents a scalable patch of neocortex containing canonical features of neocortical circuitry.
claims.source: As such, HNN's underlying neocortical network represents a scalable patch of neocortex containing canonical features of neocortical circuitry (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the design of HNN's network model and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The primary electrical current that generates EEG/MEG signals comes from synchronous activity in pyramidal neuron (PN) dendrites across a large population.
claims.source: Given that the primary electrical current that generates EEG/MEG signals comes from synchronous activity in pyramidal neuron (PN) dendrites across a large population, there are several key features of neocortical circuitry that are essential to consider when simulating these currents.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles of EEG/MEG generation.

claims.claim: Many features of neocortical circuits are remarkably similar across cortical areas and species.
claims.source: While there are known differences in microscale circuitry across cortical areas and species, many features of neocortical circuits are remarkably similar.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claims.claim: Conserved features of neocortical circuits are minimally sufficient to account for the generation of evoked responses and brain rhythms measured with EEG/MEG.
claims.source: We assume these conserved features are minimally sufficient to account for the generation of evoked responses and brain rhythms measured with EEG/MEG, and we have harnessed this generalization into HNN's foundational model, with success in simulating many of these signals using the same template model (see Introduction).
claims.evidence: This is an assumption underlying the HNN model design, supported by inference from prior successful applications.

claims.claim: HNN's template circuit includes a 3-layered structure with pyramidal neurons in the supragranular and infragranular layers whose dendrites span across the layers and are synaptically coupled to inhibitory interneurons in a 3-to-1 ratio of pyramidal to inhibitory cells.
claims.source: A 3-layered structure with pyramidal neurons in the supragranular and infragranular layers whose dendrites span across the layers and are synaptically coupled to inhibitory interneurons in a 3-to-1 ratio of pyramidal to inhibitory cells (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of HNN's template circuit and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Cells in the granular layer are not explicitly included in the template circuit.
claims.source: Of note, cells in the granular layer are not explicitly included in the template circuit.
claims.evidence: This describes a design choice in the HNN model.

claims.claim: Macroscale current dipoles are dominated by PN activity in supragranular and infragranular layers.
claims.source: This initial design choice was based on the fact that macroscale current dipoles are dominated by PN activity in supragranular and infragranular layers.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles and justifies a design choice in HNN.

claims.claim: Thalamic input to granular layers is presumed to propagate directly to basal and oblique dendrites of PN in the supragranular and infragranular layers.
claims.source: Thalamic input to granular layers is presumed to propagate directly to basal and oblique dendrites of PN in the supragranular and infragranular layers.
claims.evidence: This is an assumption in the HNN model based on knowledge of cortical circuitry.

claims.claim: The number of cells in the HNN network is adjustable while maintaining a 3-to-1 pyramidal to inhibitory interneuron ratio in each layer.
claims.source: The number of cells in the network is adjustable in the Local Network Parameters window via the Cells tab, while maintaining at 3-to-1 pyramidal to inhibitory interneuron ratio in each layer.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN software.

claims.claim: Evoked responses are typically on the order of 10 – 100nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the synchronous spiking activity of the order of tens of thousands of pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: Evoked responses are typically on the order of 10 – 100nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the synchronous spiking activity of the order of tens of thousands of pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge and estimates in the field.

claims.claim: Low-frequency oscillations are larger in magnitude and are on the order of 100–1000 nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the subthreshold activity of on the order of a million pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: Low-frequency oscillations are larger in magnitude and are on the order of 100–1000 nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the subthreshold activity of on the order of a million pyramidal neurons (Jones et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2007; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on prior work cited.

claims.claim: One type of input to HNN's model represents excitatory synaptic drive that comes from the lemniscal thalamus and contacts the cortex in the granular layers, which then propagates to the proximal PN dendrites in the supragranular and infragranular layers and somata of the inhibitory neurons; this input is referred to as proximal drive.
claims.source: One type of input represents excitatory synaptic drive that comes from the lemniscal thalamus and contacts the cortex in the granular layers, which then propagates to the proximal PN dendrites in the supragranular and infragranular layers and somata of the inhibitory neurons; this input is referred to as proximal drive (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN model and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Another input to HNN's model represents excitatory synaptic drive from higher-order cortex or non-specific thalamic nuclei that synapses directly into the supragranular layers and contacts the distal PN dendrites and somata of the inhibitory neuron; this input is referred to as distal drive.
claims.source: The other input represents excitatory synaptic drive from higher-order cortex or non-specific thalamic nuclei that synapses directly into the supragranular layers and contacts the distal PN dendrites and somata of the inhibitory neuron; this input is referred to as distal drive (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN model and is illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The networks that provide proximal and distal input to the local circuit are not explicitly modelled, but rather these inputs are represented by simulated trains of action potentials that activate excitatory post-synaptic receptors in the local network.
claims.source: The networks that provide proximal and distal input to the local circuit (e.g., thalamus and higher order cortex) are not explicitly modelled, but rather these inputs are represented by simulated trains of action potentials that activate excitatory post-synaptic receptors in the local network.
claims.evidence: This describes a design choice in the HNN model.

claims.claim: The timing and the strength of the exogenous drive to the local network were the only parameters that were originally tuned to simulate ERPs and oscillations.
claims.source: All of these equations and parameters were then fixed, and the only parameters that were originally tuned to simulate ERPs and oscillations were the timing and the strength of the exogenous drive to the local network.
claims.evidence: This describes the parameter tuning approach used in developing HNN.

claims.claim: The biophysical constraints on the origin of the current dipoles signal will dictate the output of the model and necessarily limit the space of parameter adjustments that can accurately account for the recorded data.
claims.source: Importantly, the biophysical constraints on the origin of the current dipoles signal (discussed above) will dictate the output of the model and necessarily limit the space of parameter adjustments that can accurately account for the recorded data.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about how biophysical constraints affect model behavior.

claims.claim: A parameter sensitivity analysis on perturbations around the default ERP parameter sets confirmed that a subset of the parameters have the strongest influence on features of the ERP waveform.
claims.source: A parameter sensitivity analysis on perturbations around the default ERP parameter sets confirmed that a subset of the parameters have the strongest influence on features of the ERP waveform (see Supplementary Materials).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from sensitivity analysis presented in supplementary materials.

claims.claim: HNN's interactive GUI is designed for users with no formal computational neural modeling or software development experience to be able to develop and test hypotheses on the cellular- and circuit-level generators of their human data.
claims.source: HNN's interactive GUI is designed for users with no formal computational neural modeling or software development experience to be able to develop and test hypotheses on the cellular- and circuit-level generators of their human data.
claims.evidence: This describes the design goal of HNN.

claims.claim: The template network model contains features of a canonical neocortical circuit, with layer-specific thalamocortical and cortico-cortical drive, where the net primary current dipoles are simulated from the intracellular current across the network of pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: The template network model contains features of a canonical neocortical circuit, with layer-specific thalamocortical and cortico-cortical drive, where the net primary current dipoles are simulated from the intracellular current across the network of pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of HNN's template model.

claims.claim: HNN led to a novel prediction on the origin of transient neocortical beta oscillations, and the prediction was later tested and supported by laminar recordings in mice and monkeys.
claims.source: As one specific example, HNN led to a novel prediction on the origin of transient neocortical beta oscillations, and the prediction was later tested and supported by laminar recordings in mice and monkeys (Sherman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior publication that validated model predictions.

claims.claim: The scalability of HNN provides an unprecedented framework for translational neuroscience research.
claims.source: Overall, the scalability of HNN provides an unprecedented framework for translational neuroscience research.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the utility of HNN based on inference from its design features.

claims.claim: HNN's model is unique compared to other EEG/MEG modeling software.
claims.source: This construction is unique compared to other EEG/MEG modeling software (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative claim that is elaborated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The tactile evoked response could be reproduced in HNN by 'activating' the network with a sequence of layer-specific proximal and distal spike train drive to the local network.
claims.source: In prior publications, we showed that this tactile evoked response could be reproduced in HNN by 'activating' the network with a sequence of layer-specific proximal and distal spike train drive to the local network, which is distributed with HNN in the file 'ERPYes100Trials.param'.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior published work and data included with HNN.

claims.claim: The sequence of drive that accurately reproduced the tactile evoked response consisted of 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~25 ms post stimulus, followed by 'feedback'/distal input at ~60 ms, followed by a subsequent 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~125 ms.
claims.source: The drive sequence that accurately reproduced the tactile evoked response consisted of 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~25 ms post stimulus, followed by 'feedback'/distal input at ~60 ms, followed by a subsequent 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~125 ms (Gaussian distribution of input times on each simulated trial, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This describes the specific drive sequence used to reproduce the evoked response and is illustrated in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A scaling factor was applied to net dipole output to match to the magnitude of the recorded ERP data and used to predict the number of neurons contributing to the recorded ERP.
claims.source: Note, a scaling factor was applied to net dipole output to match to the magnitude of the recorded ERP data and used to predict the number of neurons contributing to the recorded ERP.
claims.evidence: This describes a method used in HNN to relate model output to data.

claims.claim: In the tactile evoked response example, 600,000 neurons contributed to the evoked response.
claims.source: In this case, since there are 100 pyramidal neurons in each of layers 2/3 and 5, that amounts to 600,000 neurons (200 neurons x 3000 scaling factor) contributing to the evoked response, consistent with the experimental literature (described in Jones et al., 2009 and Jones et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a calculation based on the scaling factor applied in the model and is consistent with cited literature.

claims.claim: Alpha rhythms in neocortex rely on ~10 Hz bursting in the thalamus.
claims.source: Motivated by a long history of research showing alpha rhythms in neocortex rely on ~10 Hz bursting in the thalamus, we tested the hypothesis that ~10 Hz bursts of drive through proximal and distal projection pathways (representing lemniscal and non-lemniscal thalamic drive) could reproduce an alpha rhythm in the local circuit.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: When ~ 10 Hz bursts of proximal and distal drives are subthreshold and arrive to the local network in anti-phase (~50 ms delay) a pure alpha rhythm emerges.
claims.source: We showed that when ~ 10 Hz bursts of proximal and distal drives are subthreshold and arrive to the local network in anti-phase (~50 ms delay) a pure alpha rhythm emerges (Jones et al., 2009; Ziegler et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior publications.

claims.claim: Brief bouts of beta activity ('beta events') non-time locked to alpha events could be generated by decreasing the mean delay between the proximal and distal drive to 0 ms and increasing the strength of the distal drive relative to the proximal drive.
claims.source: By hand tuning the parameters we were able to match the output of the model to several features of the recorded data, including symmetric amplitude modulation around zero and PSD plots as shown in Figures 7 and 8 (see further feature matching in Jones et al., 2009 and Sherman et al., 2016), we arrived at the hypothesis that brief bouts of beta activity ('beta events') non-time locked to alpha events could be generated by decreasing the mean delay between the proximal and distal drive to 0 ms and increasing the strength of the distal drive relative to the proximal drive.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis developed through model tuning and is illustrated in Figures 7 and 8.

claims.claim: Beta events emerge on cycles when the two stochastic drives hit the network simultaneously and when the distal drive is strong enough to break the upward flowing current and create a prominent ~50 ms downward deflection.
claims.source: With this mechanism, beta events emerged on cycles when the two stochastic drives hit the network simultaneously and when the distal drive was strong enough to break the upward flowing current and create a prominent ~50 ms downward deflection (see red box in Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of beta event generation in the model and is illustrated in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The beta event hypothesis was purely model derived and was based on matching several features of the SI mu rhythm between the model output and data.
claims.source: This beta event hypothesis was purely model derived and was based on matching several features of the SI mu rhythm between the model output and data (detailed in Jones et al., 2009 Sherman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the origin of the beta event hypothesis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Model derived predictions on mechanisms underlying alpha and beta were motivated by literature and further refined by tuning the parameters to match the output of the model with various features of the recorded data.
claims.source: The model derived predictions on mechanisms underlying alpha and beta where motivated by literature and further refined by tuning the parameters to match the output of the model with various features of the recorded data.
claims.evidence: This describes the process used to develop predictions with HNN.

claims.claim: One specific prediction was that the orientation of the current during the prominent ~50 ms deflection defining a beta event was down the pyramidal neuron dendrites (e.g. into the cortex).
claims.source: One specific prediction was that the orientation of the current during the prominent ~50 ms deflection defining a beta event (red box, Figure 8B) was down the pyramidal neuron dendrites (e.g. into the cortex).
claims.evidence: This is a specific prediction from the model illustrated in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Predictions on beta events were subsequently tested and validated with laminar recordings in both mice and monkeys, where it was also confirmed that features of beta events are conserved across species and recording modalities.
claims.source: This prediction, along with several others, were subsequently tested and validated with laminar recordings in both mice and monkeys, where it was also confirmed that features of beta events are conserved across species and recording modalities (Sherman et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to publications that validated model predictions.

claims.claim: Low gamma rhythms in the 30–80 Hz range can emerge in local spiking networks through excitatory and inhibitory cell interactions where synaptic time constants set the frequency of the oscillation.
claims.source: It has been well established through experiments and computational modeling that these rhythms can emerge in local spiking networks through excitatory and inhibitory cell interactions where synaptic time constants set the frequency of the oscillation, while broadband or 'high gamma' rhythms reflect spiking activity in the network that creates sharp waveform deflections (Lee and Jones, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge and is supported by citation.

claims.claim: The period of the low gamma oscillation is determined by the time constant of decay of GABAA-mediated inhibitory currents.
claims.source: The period of the low gamma oscillation is determined by the time constant of decay of GABAA-mediated inhibitory currents (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010), a mechanism that has been referred to as pyramidal-interneuron gamma (PING).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gamma oscillations.

claims.claim: In normal regimes, the decay time constant of GABAA-mediated synapses (~25 ms) bounds oscillations to the low gamma frequency band (~40 Hz).
claims.source: In normal regimes, the decay time constant of GABAA-mediated synapses (~25 ms) bounds oscillations to the low gamma frequency band (~40 Hz).
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claims.claim: PING rhythms are initiated by 'excitation' to the excitatory (PN) cells, and this initial excitation causes PN spiking that, in turn, synaptically activates a spiking population of inhibitory (I) cells.
claims.source: In general, PING rhythms are initiated by 'excitation' to the excitatory (PN) cells, and this initial excitation causes PN spiking that, in turn, synaptically activates a spiking population of inhibitory (I) cells.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of PING rhythms based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: HNN was applied to determine if features in the current dipole signal could distinguish PING-mediated gamma from other possible mechanisms such as exogenous rhythmic drive or spiking activity that creates 'high gamma' oscillations.
claims.source: We have applied HNN to determine if features in the current dipole signal could distinguish PING-mediated gamma from other possible mechanisms such as exogenous rhythmic drive or spiking activity that creates 'high gamma' oscillations (Lee and Jones, 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes an application of HNN and is supported by citation.

claims.claim: To improve the fit to the suprathreshold evoked response data, a procedure for sequentially optimizing the strengths of the proximal and distal drive inputs generating the evoked response can be run.
claims.source: To improve the fit to the data, a procedure for sequentially optimizing the strengths of the proximal and distal drive inputs generating the evoked response can be run.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of HNN's optimization procedure.

claims.claim: The RMSE between the data and the model improved from 30.53 to 15.54 after optimization for the suprathreshold evoked response.
claims.source: Here, the simulation from the optimized parameter set for the suprathreshold evoked response is shown in gray with an improved RMSE of 15.54 compared to 30.53 for the initial model.
claims.evidence: This is data from the optimization example shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: HNN is a neural modeling software tool developed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origin of their human EEG or MEG data.
claims.source: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN, https://hnn.brown.edu) is a neural modeling software tool developed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origin of their human EEG or MEG data.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about HNN.

claims.claim: The tutorials and the example workflow focus on studying the neural origin of ERPs and low-frequency oscillations from a single brain region.
claims.source: Based on prior applications of HNN's underlying template neural model on these signals (Jones et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2007; Khan et al., 2015; Lee and Jones, 2013; Sherman et al., 2016; Sliva et al., 2018; Ziegler et al., 2010), the tutorials and the example workflow focus on studying the neural origin of ERPs and low-frequency oscillations from a single brain region.
claims.evidence: This describes the focus of HNN's tutorials and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: HNN enables visualization and direct comparison of the primary current dipole produced by the network to source-localized data in units of Am, under various parameter manipulations.
claims.source: HNN enables visualization and direct comparison of the primary current dipole produced by the network to source-localized data in units of Am, under various parameter manipulations.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of HNN.

claims.claim: HNN was created based on the biophysical origin of EEG/MEG primary currents to be a hypothesis development and testing tool.
claims.source: HNN was created based on the biophysical origin of EEG/MEG primary currents to be a hypothesis development and testing tool, where specific predictions on the microcircuit-level underpinnings of recorded data can be produced.
claims.evidence: This describes the design philosophy of HNN.

claims.claim: The circuit-level predictions from HNN can guide further validation with invasive recordings or with other imaging modalities.
claims.source: The circuit-level predictions can guide further validation with invasive recordings or with other imaging modalities (e.g., spectroscopy or tractography, see Khan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the intended use of HNN and is supported by citation to an example.

claims.claim: HNN is particularly timely given the rapidly expanding wealth of genetic insights and phenotype data in animal model systems.
claims.source: HNN is particularly timely given the rapidly expanding wealth of genetic insights and phenotype data in animal model systems.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the timeliness of HNN based on current trends in neuroscience.

claims.claim: As disease-specific genetic mutations and corresponding cellular/circuit outcomes in mouse models are identified, they can be implemented in HNN, and their impact on EEG/MEG measured brain dynamics can be simulated.
claims.source: As disease-specific genetic mutations and corresponding cellular/circuit outcomes in mouse models are identified, they can be implemented in HNN, and their impact on EEG/MEG measured brain dynamics, ranging from ongoing state properties (e.g., alpha oscillations) to sensory-evoked responses, can be simulated.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential application of HNN based on speculation about future use.

claims.claim: Among current modeling software designed specifically for study of EEG/MEG signals, HNN's model, goals, and capabilities are unique.
claims.source: Among the current modeling software designed specifically for study of EEG/MEG signals (e.g., The Virtual Brain [TVB] https://thevirtualbrain.org, Dynamic Causal Modeling [DCM] of E/MEG within the Statistical Parametric Mapping [SPM] software https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/, and LFPy https://lfpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/; Hagen et al., 2018; Kiebel et al., 2008; Sanz Leon et al., 2013), HNN's model, goals, and capabilities are unique.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative claim about HNN relative to other software.

claims.claim: The goal of HNN is to provide a user-friendly graphical interface to a validated biophysically detailed model of neocortical circuitry, and to teach the community, regardless of neural modeling or coding experience, how to interact with the model to study the neural origin of commonly measured macroscale EEG/MEG signals.
claims.source: The goal of HNN is to provide a user-friendly graphical interface to a validated biophysically detailed model of neocortical circuitry, and to teach the community, regardless of neural modeling or coding experience, how to interact with the model to study the neural origin of commonly measured macroscale EEG/MEG signals.
claims.evidence: This describes the goal of HNN.

claims.claim: LFPy is a Python package that provides a set of Python libraries and associated documentation on how to apply these scripts to simulate multi-scale signals, including current dipole, LFP, ECoG, M/EEG sensor signals, in user defined multi-compartment neuron models and networks built in NEURON or NeuroML.
claims.source: LFPy is a Python package that provides a set of Python libraries and associated documentation on how to apply these scripts to simulate multi-scale signals, including current dipole, LFP, ECoG, M/EEG sensor signals, in user defined multi-compartment neuron models and networks built in NEURON or NeuroML (Hagen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes LFPy software and is supported by citation.

claims.claim: LFPy does not contain a GUI and is designed for users who have experience in neural modeling and Python.
claims.source: LFPy does not contain a GUI and is designed for users who have experience in neural modeling and Python.
claims.evidence: This is a factual description of LFPy software.

claims.claim: DCM applied to EEG/MEG data is a non-GUI based scripting tool, using Matlab.
claims.source: DCM applied to EEG/MEG data is also a non-GUI based scripting tool, using Matlab.
claims.evidence: This is a factual description of DCM software.

claims.claim: In DCM, users assume an active set of distributed sites, that is nodes, in the brain that contribute to a recorded signal.
claims.source: Users assume an active set of distributed sites, that is nodes, in the brain that contribute to a recorded signal.
claims.evidence: This describes how DCM is used.

claims.claim: In DCM, the neural activity of a node is simulated using 'neural mass' representations in which the activity (e.g. firing rate) of a population of neurons is simulated with a reduced number of variables.
claims.source: The neural activity of a node is simulated using 'neural mass' representations in which the activity (e.g. firing rate) of a population of neurons is simulated with a reduced number of variables (Kiebel et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This describes DCM methodology and is supported by citation.

claims.claim: TVB is designed to simulate large-scale network interactions using reduced neural mass representations.
claims.source: TVB is designed to simulate large-scale network interactions also using reduced neural mass representations.
claims.evidence: This is a factual description of TVB software.

claims.claim: In TVB, active nodes across the whole brain are assumed to contribute to the recorded signal and connectivity between nodes is informed by individualized tractography data.
claims.source: Active nodes across the whole brain are assumed to contribute to the recorded signal and connectivity between nodes is informed by individualized tractography data (Sanz Leon et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes TVB methodology and is supported by citation.

claims.claim: One advantage of TVB's approach is that propagation of activity across the brain can be studied (e.g. spread of seizure), unlike HNN which is currently restricted to interpreting detailed activity in a single region of interest.
claims.source: One advantage of this approach is that propagation of activity across the brain can be studied (e.g. spread of seizure), unlike HNN which is currently restricted to interpreting detailed activity in a single region of interest.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement about TVB and HNN capabilities.

claims.claim: Many prior models of EEG/MEG rely on reduced representations of neural activity, including neural mass and/or mean field approximations.
claims.source: Indeed, many prior models of EEG/MEG rely on reduced representations of neural activity, including neural mass and/or mean field approximations (Breakspear et al., 2004; Jansen and Rit, 1995; Jirsa and Haken, 1996; Kiebel et al., 2008; Sanz Leon et al., 2013; Woolrich and Stephan, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about EEG/MEG modeling approaches supported by citations.

claims.claim: Simplifications in neural models may be necessary to ensure mathematical or computational tractability of models that address interactions between multiple areas or whole brain activity.
claims.source: Such simplifications may be necessary to ensure mathematical or computational tractability of models that address interactions between multiple areas or whole brain activity (Breakspear, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about modeling tradeoffs supported by citation.

claims.claim: Tractability of reduced models comes at the cost of suppressing or eliminating the ability to evaluate cellular-level details of individual spiking units and dendritic currents, or to perform one-to-one comparisons between model and data.
claims.source: However, that tractability comes at the cost of suppressing or eliminating the ability to evaluate cellular-level details of individual spiking units and dendritic currents, or to perform one-to-one comparisons between model and data; explicit goals of HNN.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about tradeoffs in modeling approaches.

claims.claim: HNN's model was chosen to be minimally sufficient to accurately account for the biophysical origin of the primary currents that underlie EEG/MEG signals in a single brain area.
claims.source: HNN's model was chosen to be minimally sufficient to accurately account for the biophysical origin of the primary currents that underlie EEG/MEG signals in a single brain area; namely, the net intracellular current flow in the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons that span across the cortical layers and receive layer-specific synaptic input from other brain areas.
claims.evidence: This describes the design philosophy of HNN's model.

claims.claim: HNN's model was constructed to maintain known canonical features of neocortical circuitry including, excitatory/inhibitory ratios, layer specific synaptic interactions, and cell spiking behaviors.

claims.claim: HNN's model has been successful in interpreting the origin of extracranially measured macro-scale EEG/MEG signals that likely rely on canonical macroscale features of neocortical circuitry and not on finer details of the underlying structure.

claims.source: In Bush and Sejnowski (1993), digitized HRP-filled pyramidal neurons from layers 2 and 5 of cat visual cortex consisting of 400 compartments were reduced to 8 and 9 compartments, respectively.

claims.claim: In HNN, a scaling factor of 1.3 was applied to the length and diameters of the dendritic compartments to account for increases in dendritic length and volume in human somatosensory neurons.
claims.source: In HNN, a scaling factor of 1.3 was applied to the length and diameters of the dendritic compartments to account for increases in dendritic length and volume in human somatosensory neurons, as predicted by larger cortical thickness (Fischl and Dale, 2000; Geyer et al., 1997) and an increase in the number of dendritic spines and arborization (Elston et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This describes a modification made in HNN and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Membrane voltages in each simulated compartment were calculated using the standard Hodgkin-Huxley parallel conductance equations.
claims.source: Membrane voltages in each simulated compartment were calculated using the standard Hodgkin-Huxley parallel conductance equations, and current flow between compartments follows from cable theory as accounted for in NEURON.
claims.evidence: This describes the biophysical equations used in HNN.

claims.claim: Active ionic currents were included in both the somatic and dendritic compartment of the cells of the pyramidal neurons, and in the single compartment of the inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Extending the prior work of Bush and Sejnowski (1993), active ionic currents were included in both the somatic and dendritic compartment of the cells of the pyramidal neurons, and in the single compartment of the inhibitory neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the biophysical detail in HNN's model.

claims.claim: The maximal conductances of each current were constant throughout the soma and dendrite.
claims.source: The maximal conductances of each current were constant throughout the soma and dendrite (Bekkers, 2000; Korngreen and Sakmann, 2000; Migliore and Shepherd, 2002; Stuart and Sakmann, 1994) and were chosen to produce adapting spikes in the L2/3 PNs and bursting in the L5 PNs to current injected in the soma (1 nA for 100 ms) representative of neurons classified as regular spiking and intrinsically bursting, respectively (Moore and Nelson, 1998; Silva et al., 1991; Zhu and Connors, 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes parameter choices in HNN's model and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The inhibitory neurons were tuned to represent basket cells and produced regular fast spiking dynamics to injected current.
claims.source: The inhibitory neurons were tuned to represent basket cells and produced regular fast spiking dynamics to injected current, as in other cortical network models (Garabedian et al., 2003; Jones et al., 2000; Pinto et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This describes the tuning of inhibitory neurons in HNN and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Inhibitory synaptic connections onto PNs were located on the soma.
claims.source: Inhibitory synaptic connections onto PNs were located on the soma (Freund et al., 1986; Kisvárday et al., 1985; Somogyi et al., 1983), and excitatory synapses contacted the basal and apical oblique dendrites (Deuchars et al., 1994; Feldmeyer et al., 2002; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson and Bannister, 1998).

claims.source: Synaptic dynamics were modeled with bi-exponential functions.

claims.source: There is all-to-all connectivity between any two populations of synaptically-coupled neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the connectivity pattern in HNN's model.

claims.claim: Axial current flow between any two neighboring model compartments i,j is defined as iaxial = (vi - vj)/raxial.
claims.source: Axial current flow between any two neighboring model compartments i,j is defined as iaxial = (vi - vj)/raxial, where vi, vj, and raxial are the voltages in compartment i, j, and the resistance between the compartments, respectively.
claims.evidence: This describes the calculation of axial current in HNN.

claims.claim: To convert axial current into a dipole signal, a length scaling is applied where the axial current is scaled by the inter-compartment distance along the vertical axis.
claims.source: In order to convert this axial current into a dipole signal, we apply a length scaling where the axial current is scaled by the inter-compartment distance along the vertical axis.
claims.evidence: This describes the method for calculating dipole signals in HNN.

claims.claim: The contribution from all neighboring compartments within a neuron is integrated and then added to a value across the set of all pyramidal neurons to produce the model dipole output signal.
claims.source: The contribution from all neighboring compartments within a neuron is integrated and then added to a value across the set of all pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes how the net dipole is calculated in HNN.

claims.claim: As a result of the multiplication between axial current and length, the model dipole output signal has the same units of measure as the experimental data (Am).
claims.source: As a result of the multiplication between axial current and length, the model dipole output signal has the same units of measure as the experimental data (Am) (Okada et al., 1997; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Jones et al., 2007; Hagen et al., 2018).

claims.source: HNN includes a method to optimize ERP simulations. The optimization procedure was uniquely designed to minimize the RMSE between model output and ERP waveforms in a stepwise manner that decreases parameter exploration and saves compute time.

claims.source: This procedure takes advantage of the assumption that the exogenous proximal and distal driving inputs are essential parameters to tune to get an accurate representation of an ERP waveform.

results.result: MEG/EEG are the only noninvasive methods to study electrical neural activity in humans with millisecond resolution and provide biomarkers of healthy and abnormal brain dynamics, but relating these macroscopic signals to underlying cellular- and circuit-level generators is a major limitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6, and C7 establish the capabilities of MEG/EEG based on established knowledge in the field. Claims C2 and C8 identify the interpretability limitation, which is well-recognized in the neuroscience community. These claims are mutually consistent and supported by established knowledge.

results.result: HNN is a neural modeling software tool with a graphical user interface that enables researchers and clinicians without coding experience to interpret the neural origins of MEG/EEG by simulating primary current dipoles from a canonical neocortical circuit model with biophysically realistic neurons, producing output in the same units (Am) as source-localized data.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C9-C11, C16, C47, C71, and C79 consistently describe HNN's design, features, and capabilities. The biophysical basis (C10) is supported by multiple citations. The key innovation of the GUI (C16) and the matching units between model and data (C11, C28) are clearly documented features that enable the stated goal of accessibility to non-experts.

results.result: HNN's underlying model has been successfully applied in prior publications to interpret sensory evoked responses and oscillations in alpha, beta, and gamma bands, leading to novel predictions about beta oscillations that were subsequently validated with laminar recordings in mice and monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 document prior applications supported by multiple citations. Claims C49, C60, C62, and C63 describe a specific example where HNN generated a novel prediction about beta oscillations that was later validated experimentally (Sherman et al., 2016). The tactile evoked response example (C52, C53, C55) demonstrates successful reproduction of experimental data. This represents a complete cycle of hypothesis generation and experimental validation.

results.result: HNN is designed as a hypothesis development and testing tool to produce circuit-level predictions that can be tested with invasive recordings or other imaging modalities, providing a framework for translational neuroscience research, particularly for implementing disease-specific genetic mutations from animal models.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C74, and C75 describe HNN's intended purpose as a hypothesis testing tool, supported by the validation example in C49/C63. Claims C29 and C48 clarify the current scope (single region). Claims C50, C76, and C77 discuss translational potential, though C77 is speculative about future applications. The core claim about hypothesis testing is well-supported by design features and prior validation.

results.result: HNN simulates primary currents (Jp) that generate MEG/EEG signals based on established electromagnetic biophysics, calculating current dipoles from intracellular current flow in pyramidal neuron dendrites oriented normal to the cortical mantle, producing output in ampere-meters (Am) that matches source-localized data units.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 describe the biophysical basis of MEG/EEG generation, supported by multiple citations to established work. Claims C27, C28, and C130 describe how HNN implements this biophysics to produce output in matching units (Am). The mathematical formulation (C127-C130) is clearly described and based on established cable theory and electromagnetic principles.

results.result: HNN's template model represents a canonical neocortical circuit with conserved features across cortical areas and species, including a 3-layered structure with pyramidal neurons and interneurons in a 3:1 ratio, which is minimally sufficient to account for generation of evoked responses and brain rhythms measured with EEG/MEG.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 describe the canonical circuit structure based on established neuroscience knowledge (C32). The design assumption (C33) that conserved features are sufficient is supported by prior successful applications (C12, C93). Claims C34-C40 provide specific architectural details. The justification for excluding granular layer cells (C35-C37) is based on biophysical principles (C36). Claims C91-C93 articulate the design philosophy and its success.

results.result: HNN models layer-specific exogenous inputs as proximal drive (lemniscal thalamus to basal/oblique dendrites) and distal drive (higher-order cortex/non-lemniscal thalamus to distal dendrites), with the timing and strength of these drives being the critical parameters for simulating ERPs, as confirmed by sensitivity analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 describe the two types of exogenous drive based on known anatomy. Claim C44 documents the parameter tuning approach used in model development. Claims C45-C46 and C95 establish that drive timing and strength are critical parameters, supported by sensitivity analysis in supplementary materials. Claim C96 describes the optimization tool based on these insights. The approach is methodologically sound and well-documented.

results.result: HNN simulations predict that alpha rhythms emerge from ~10 Hz bursts of proximal and distal drive arriving in anti-phase, while beta events emerge when these drives arrive simultaneously with strong distal input, creating downward current flow; these predictions were validated with laminar recordings in mice and monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 establishes the literature basis for alpha mechanisms. Claims C57-C59 describe specific model predictions about alpha and beta generation mechanisms developed through parameter tuning (C61). Claims C60 and C62 specify the novel prediction about beta events. Claim C63 documents experimental validation in multiple species. This represents a complete hypothesis-testing cycle with cross-species validation.

results.result: HNN was applied to study PING-mediated gamma oscillations (30-80 Hz), which emerge through excitatory-inhibitory cell interactions with the period determined by GABAA decay time constants (~25 ms), bounding oscillations to ~40 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 describe the established PING mechanism for gamma oscillations, supported by citations (C64, C65). Claim C68 documents HNN's application to distinguish PING-mediated gamma from other mechanisms. The biophysical basis is well-established in the literature, and HNN's implementation follows known principles.

results.result: HNN includes an optimization procedure that sequentially optimizes exogenous drive parameters to minimize RMSE between model and data, using the COBYLA algorithm with temporal weighting based on input timing, improving RMSE from 30.53 to 15.54 in the suprathreshold evoked response example.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 describe the optimization method's design and implementation. The stepwise approach (C131, C132) is justified by the assumption that drive parameters are critical (C132) and temporal causality (C133). The specific example (C69, C70) demonstrates quantitative improvement. The choice of COBYLA algorithm (C134, C135) is justified by comparative performance. The method is well-documented with concrete results.

results.result: HNN's model, goals, and capabilities are unique among EEG/MEG modeling software (LFPy, DCM, TVB) because it provides a user-friendly GUI to a biophysically detailed model that enables cellular-level interpretation and one-to-one data comparison, whereas other tools use reduced neural mass representations or require coding expertise.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C87 provide factual descriptions of other software tools (LFPy, DCM, TVB) and their differences from HNN. Claims C88-C90 discuss the tradeoffs between model complexity and tractability. The comparative analysis is fair and acknowledges both advantages (C87) and limitations of different approaches. The uniqueness claim (C78) is supported by the specific differences documented.

results.result: HNN was used to test hypotheses about tACS-induced modulation of synaptic dynamics by comparing pre- and post-tACS EEG signals, and future expansions will include direct simulation of NIBS-induced fields coupled to modeled neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 describes a demonstrated application shown in Figure 5. Claims C105 and C106 describe planned future expansions that are clearly labeled as speculative. The current application is supported by data, while future directions are appropriately qualified as plans.

results.result: Future expansions of HNN include simulating LFPs and sensor-level signals, optimizing additional parameters, converting to NetPyNe for multi-area modeling, and integrating with MNE software for source localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C97, C99, C101, C102, and C103 describe planned future developments that are clearly speculative. Claim C98 documents current availability on high-performance computing platforms. While the plans are reasonable and well-motivated, they represent intentions rather than completed work. The current capabilities (C98) are supported, but future expansions cannot be evaluated as results.

results.result: HNN is distributed online at hnn.brown.edu with installation options for multiple operating systems, implemented in NEURON with Python and MPI parallelization, using neuron morphologies adapted from Bush and Sejnowski (1993) with scaling for human neurons, and synaptic connectivity based on rodent somatosensory cortex studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 provide factual information about distribution and implementation. Claims C112-C113 document the source of neuron morphologies with proper citation. Claim C115 describes the scaling factor applied for human neurons, supported by citations. Claims C116-C125 describe the biophysical and network implementation details. Claims C127-C129 describe the dipole calculation method. All implementation details are clearly documented with appropriate citations.

results.result: The complexity of the original model and code hindered community use, and HNN's construction is unique compared to other EEG/MEG modeling software.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 is an inference about barriers to adoption of the prior version, which motivated development of the GUI (C16). Claim C51 asserts uniqueness, which is elaborated and supported in the Discussion section (C78-C90). Both claims are reasonable inferences supported by the comparative analysis and the design choices made in HNN.
